burton_span.exact: But when the face of Heaven changed is / To tempests, rain, from season fair: / Our minds are altered, and in our breasts / Forthwith some new conceits appear.

1.2.2.5-f17.text: Verum ubi tempestas, & coeli mobilis humor / Mutavere vices, & Jupiter humidus Austro, / Vertuntur species animorum, & pectore motus / Concipiunt alios ———

translations.literal: But when the weather and the sky's mobile moisture / have changed turns, and Jupiter wet with the South wind, / the aspects of minds are turned, and in the breast motions / they conceive other —
translations.note: Here humor means the moisture of the sky, not a bodily humour. The standard text of Virgil, Georgics 1.417–420, reads 'mutavere vias' (changed their courses), not 'vices'; 'Iuppiter uvidus Austris' (south winds, plural), not 'humidus Austro'; and 'pectora', not 'pectore'. Burton also leaves out line 419 ('denset erant quae rara modo, et quae densa relaxat', which supplies the verb for Jupiter), so 'Jupiter humidus Austro' has no verb in his version. The quotation breaks off at 'alios'.

translations.text: But when the weather and the shifting moisture of the sky / have changed their turns, and Jupiter is wet with the south wind, / the moods of minds are altered, and in the breast / they conceive other impulses —

translations.note: Coeli humor is moisture of the sky (weather), not a bodily humour. Burton's English verse that follows is a loose rendering. Virgil is not named in the text immediately here, but the 'before' text says 'This was Virgil's experiment'.

translations.text: But when the weather and the changeable moisture of the sky / Have changed their courses, and Jupiter is wet with the South wind, / The appearances of minds are turned, and their breasts / Conceive other emotions ———
